CivicOps AI · Group 23 · External Factors component

Critical Facility Proximity

A transparent, offline, rule-based geographic factor that tells the Urgency component whether a NYC311 request is adjacent to a hospital, school, childcare centre, senior-care home, fire station or police station. The report covers acquisition, methodology, threshold research, validation and packaging.

Generated 2026-10-16 · ruleset 1.0.0 · OSM data nyc-osm-2026-10-15 · component v1.0.0

1. Executive summary

100 mselected threshold, all six core categories
27.3%historical requests flagged 1 (all splits)
2.5%incomplete, returned as null (never 0)
4,445de-duplicated OSM facilities, 5 boroughs + 2 km
90/90automated tests executed, 0 failed
0.14 msmedian single-request latency (offline)

What the factor represents. external_factor = 1 means that, after a valid and complete evaluation, at least one qualifying critical facility's mapped geometry lies within 100 m (straight line, inclusive) of the request location. In operational terms, the request is on the facility's block frontage, directly across the street, or at the adjacent intersection. 0 means no qualifying facility is that close. null means the component could not decide safely (missing or unresolved coordinates, coarse precision, or an uncertainty interval that straddles the threshold). The factor is geographic evidence only. It is not urgency, priority or a dispatch decision.

Why 100 m is defensible. The value is a knowledge-based prior from NYC street geometry. It was checked against five criteria declared before validation results existed, and it passed all of them on validation: flag rate 26.2%, decision agreement 96.5% and positive stability 92.6% under a 15 m location error, train-validation shift -2.6 pp, and borough ratio 2.95. On the untouched test split the frozen value behaved the same way: 26.3% flagged, a shift of +0.12 pp, within the ±5 pp tolerance. The value is not statistically optimal and not an official NYC rule, because no labelled outcomes exist to optimise against.

How double counting is avoided. The default PURE_GEOGRAPHIC mode never reads the request type. The output has no urgency fields (enforced by tests). A separate critical_facility_nearby field lets Urgency combine proximity with its own request-type rules explicitly.

2. Component scope and business objective

Position in the shared flow (shared data reference): Intake bot → Emergency check → Agency and skill routing → Duplicate detection → External factors → Credibility → Fake request detection → Resolution time → Urgency → Prioritisation → Crew deployment. The component answers one question: is this request geographically adjacent to a relevant critical or sensitive facility?

Does

  • validates geolocation-enriched coordinates and their precision
  • finds nearby facilities in a local OSM cache (offline)
  • computes metric straight-line distances to point and polygon geometries
  • applies a configurable, explainable binary rule
  • returns evidence, rule identifiers and explanations
  • prepares a shared OSM road graph for Crew Dispatch

Does not

  • evaluate weather (removed from scope)
  • assign urgency, scores, weights or ranks
  • geocode addresses or invent coordinates
  • assign agencies, skills or crews
  • compute routes, travel times or run A*/Dijkstra

3. Academic course alignment

Course areaHow this component uses it
Decision automation: knowledge-based reasoningA declarative ruleset encodes domain knowledge (what counts as a critical facility, what "adjacent" means in NYC street geometry, how location uncertainty limits what can be concluded). The interval rule (decide only when the whole uncertainty disc is on one side of the threshold) is explicit reasoning under uncertainty.
Decision automation: business rulesTraceable binary decision with rule identifiers (CRITICAL_PROXIMITY_<CATEGORY>, CRITICAL_PROXIMITY_NONE, INPUT_*), versioned configuration and explanations.
Knowledge discovery and data miningDistance distributions, trigger-rate curves, elasticity, location-error robustness, borough and category sensitivity, and temporal stability on 49,558 real requests under the team's time-based split.
Business resource optimisationDeliberately not used here. Informed search belongs to Crew Dispatch, which reuses the prepared road graph.

4. Separation from the Urgency component

Urgency (Khalid) evaluates request type and other urgency factors. External Factors returns geographic evidence only.

  • Request type is not used in the default mode. A test checks that RT005 (traffic signal) and RT080 (no heat) at the same point return identical factor, evidence and rules.
  • No severity in the rules. Rule identifiers name the facility category, never a level.
  • Two fields. critical_facility_nearby is the pure geographic result. external_factor is the agreed final factor. They are identical in the selected mode. In the opt-in context-aware mode they can differ, so Urgency can always see the raw geography.
  • Forbidden output keys (urgency, priority, weight, rank, dispatch) are checked recursively by the test suite.

5. Input and output contracts

Input (geolocation-enriched request)

  • Required: request_type, latitude, longitude, geolocation_status (RESOLVED, APPROXIMATE, AMBIGUOUS, UNRESOLVED, FAILED, NOT_ATTEMPTED), location_precision (ADDRESS_POINT, GPS_DEVICE, INTERSECTION, BLOCKFACE, PLACE, POSTAL_CODE, NEIGHBORHOOD, BOROUGH, CITY, UNKNOWN)
  • Optional: request_id, borough (or slots.borough), location_source, location_uncertainty_m, location_type, ready_to_submit, needs_human, emergency_action
  • Future intake fields (accepted, never required): address_type, cross_street_2, zip_code, original_location_text, citizen_gps
  • The intake bot (CO1) sends location as text. A separate Geolocation Resolution step must add coordinates. This component never geocodes.

Output (key fields)

  • external_factor: 1 / 0 / null
  • evaluation_status: COMPLETE / INCOMPLETE, plus incomplete_reason
  • critical_facility_nearby: pure geographic evidence
  • nearest_facility_overall (any cached category, including exploratory transit), nearest_qualifying_facility and nearest_qualifying_distance_m, triggering_facilities and triggering_facility_count: three distinct notions, never mixed
  • thresholds_m, triggered_rules, explanation, location_quality (regime, margin, boundary sensitivity), warnings, needs_review
  • ruleset_version, osm_data_version, component_version

The prompt's illustrative names qualifying_facilities and qualifying_facility_count became triggering_facilities and triggering_facility_count. This keeps "qualifying category" separate from "facility that actually triggered".

6. Historical data validation

requests_real.parquet: 49,558 rows × 54 columns, all source = REAL_311, 0 synthetic rows, unique request_id: True. All 34 request types are in the catalog (34 codes). 48,401 rows have coordinates (97.7%). 3 of them fall outside the five-borough union. 58 have a borough label that differs from the coordinate borough (mostly BRONX-labelled points inside Manhattan's OSM boundary, which matches Marble Hill). 32.4% of geolocated rows repeat an earlier coordinate (repeat addresses). Counting each unique location once changes the validation trigger rate by 0.93 pp ( 26.2% per request vs 25.3% per unique location).

Rows come in borough-stratified sample windows (sample_window_id); each borough has ~10k rows, so per-borough rates are comparable but citywide rates are NOT volume-weighted to real 311 traffic.

7. OSM acquisition methodology

  • Tooling: OSMnx 2.1.1 (Overpass API + Nominatim). Boundaries via geocode_to_gdf by fixed OSM relation id. Facilities via features_from_polygon with the union of category tags. Road graph via graph_from_polygon(network_type='drive').
  • Acquired: boundaries 2026-10-15T19:50:08+00:00, facilities 2026-10-15T19:53:55+00:00, roads pending (UTC).
  • Robustness: public Overpass servers were overloaded during acquisition (HTTP 502/500, capacity errors). The downloader retries with exponential backoff across three endpoints, splits large areas into sub-queries, and caches HTTP responses, so interrupted runs resume without re-downloading.
  • Formats: GeoPackage (shareable, GIS-ready) and GeoParquet (fast runtime) for facilities. GeoPackage for boundaries. GraphML and GeoPackage for roads. manifest.json records counts, CRS, sizes and SHA-256 checksums.

9. Critical-facility selection and tagging

A category is included when it has a defensible relationship to public safety, vulnerable populations or essential emergency services. Tags and rationale live in config/facility_categories.yaml. A feature takes the first matching category in precedence order. Raw features: 4,825. 245 unclassified social facilities (shelters, food banks) were dropped. 135 duplicate representations were flagged. 0 geometries needed repair.

Excluded: clinics and doctors (no emergency-access argument), colleges and universities (adult population, land-use proxy), places of worship, libraries and community centres (a value judgement without team agreement), parks and playgrounds (area land use), ambulance stations (sparse in OSM). Exploratory: rail and subway stations are acquired and analysed but do not qualify (see §11).

10. Spatial distance methodology

  • Request lat/lon are projected to EPSG:32118 (NAD83 / New York Long Island, metres). Facilities are projected once at load.
  • Distance = GEOS planar distance from the request point to the facility's full geometry: point to point, or point to the nearest polygon boundary, and 0 inside a polygon or multipolygon. Centroids are never used.
  • A per-category STRtree returns candidates within threshold + uncertainty (plus 1 mm search slack). The decision test is inclusive (distance ≤ threshold, with 1 µm numerical tolerance).
  • Correctness: projected distances differ from WGS84 geodesic distances by at most 0.0986 m (0.00121%). Naive degree subtraction would be off by 31.8%.
  • Straight-line, not network, distance: the question is adjacency, not travel time.

Selected: Design A (pure geographic, universal threshold). Simplest configuration. Category-specific radii (B1) have no outcome evidence behind them. Transit (B2) acts as a density proxy. Request-type gating (B3) overlaps with Urgency and needs team agreement. 16.0% of Design A's validation positives are building-interior request types. Context-aware gating (B3) would zero them, and it is available as decision_mode: CONTEXT_AWARE if the Urgency owner agrees.

12. Threshold candidate selection

Operational definition. "Adjacent" means the request is in the facility's immediate surroundings: on the same block frontage, directly across the street, or at the adjacent intersection. NYC grid geometry gives the scale: short block about 80 m, avenue right-of-way about 30 m, address points up to about 30 m behind the curb. That puts adjacency at about 100 m of straight-line distance to the facility geometry. Wider radii (250 m and up) describe a neighbourhood, not adjacency.

Candidates (50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 400, 500, 750, 1000 m) are experimental values from "immediate surroundings" to "broad neighbourhood". None is presented as NYC policy. Admissible range 75–150 m: the lower bound is about 3× typical street-level geocoding error. The upper bound is where "adjacent" turns into "neighbourhood".

The selection protocol (config/threshold_selection_protocol.yaml, v1.0, fixed 2026-10-15) was written after train exploration and before any validation proximity result was computed:

  • C1 decision agreement under a 15 m displacement ≥ 95.0%
  • C2 positive stability under the same displacement ≥ 85.0%
  • C3 |validation − train| trigger rate ≤ 5.0 pp
  • C4 trigger rate ≤ 50.0% (adjacency is the minority case)
  • C5 borough max/min trigger ratio ≤ 3.0
  • Rule: Select the knowledge-based prior if it is admissible and meets C1-C5 on validation. Otherwise select the smallest admissible candidate that meets C1-C5. If none does, keep the prior and record the failed criteria as a documented limitation.

13. Threshold sensitivity results (train exploration)

The median distance from a geolocated train request to the nearest core facility is 155 m (IQR 92–256 m). Only 0.04% of requests lie inside a facility polygon. NYC is dense enough that a 250 m radius would flag 74% of requests and 500 m would flag 95%, which says almost nothing about adjacency. The curve is steepest between 100 and 150 m (elasticity 1.38 at 100 m). Schools are the nearest facility for 73% of requests.

Sensitivity to location error

Each request was displaced by exactly u metres in a random (seeded) direction and re-evaluated. Small radii are fragile relative to the number of positives. Mid radii have the most absolute flips, because most requests sit 100–200 m from a facility. Under a 120 m displacement (a blockface-level location), 24% of decisions at 100 m change. This is why coarse locations use the robust-interval regime (§17).

17. Missing-data and location-uncertainty treatment

  • Never invent coordinates, never silently return 0. Missing, invalid (out of range, non-numeric, (0,0)), unresolved, outside-coverage or too-coarse locations return external_factor = null, an explicit incomplete_reason and needs_review = true. Swapped lat/lon is reported (POSSIBLE_LAT_LON_SWAP), not repaired.
  • Uncertainty u comes from location_uncertainty_m if supplied, otherwise from a heuristic default per precision class (ADDRESS_POINT 15 m, GPS_DEVICE 20 m, INTERSECTION 25 m, BLOCKFACE 120 m, PLACE 150 m, UNKNOWN 100 m).
  • POINT_ESTIMATE (u ≤ 30 m): the supplied point decides, and boundary_sensitive flags |margin| < u. ROBUST_INTERVAL (30 < u ≤ 250 m): 1 only if margin ≥ u, 0 only if margin < −u, otherwise null. Above 250 m, or postal-code, neighbourhood or borough precision, the result is INCOMPLETE. When u exceeds the threshold, a robust positive is impossible: a location coarser than the adjacency radius cannot establish adjacency.

20. Static geographic maps

21. Urgency integration example

Synthetic request at real Manhattan coordinates (examples/near_facility.json), evaluated by the real cache. Minimal hand-off for Urgency (result.to_urgency_payload()):

{
  "request_id": "EX-NEAR-001",
  "external_factor": 1,
  "evaluation_status": "COMPLETE",
  "incomplete_reason": null,
  "critical_facility_nearby": true,
  "triggered_rules": [
    "CRITICAL_PROXIMITY_HOSPITAL",
    "LOCATION_POINT_ESTIMATE"
  ],
  "evidence": {
    "facility_category": "HOSPITAL",
    "facility_name": "The Mount Sinai Hospital",
    "distance_m": 0.0,
    "threshold_m": 100.0,
    "osm_id": "way/395304938"
  },
  "triggering_categories": [
    "HOSPITAL"
  ],
  "explanation": "A qualifying critical facility is within its configured geographic threshold: hospital 'The Mount Sinai Hospital', the request lies inside its mapped footprint (threshold 100 m). 1 other qualifying facility also within threshold (hospital). This is geographic evidence only; it does not set urgency.",
  "needs_review": false,
  "ruleset_version": "1.0.0",
  "osm_data_version": "nyc-osm-2026-10-15"
}

An incomplete request stays null with its reason, so Urgency applies its own agreed fallback (shared rule 6: a failing component must not lower anyone's score):

{
  "request_id": "EX-MISSING-001",
  "external_factor": null,
  "evaluation_status": "INCOMPLETE",
  "incomplete_reason": "MISSING_COORDINATES",
  "critical_facility_nearby": null,
  "triggered_rules": [
    "INPUT_MISSING_COORDINATES"
  ],
  "evidence": null,
  "triggering_categories": [],
  "explanation": "Evaluation incomplete (MISSING_COORDINATES): Latitude and/or longitude is missing. The factor is null, not 0, so Urgency can apply its own agreed fallback.",
  "needs_review": true,
  "ruleset_version": "1.0.0",
  "osm_data_version": "nyc-osm-2026-10-15"
}

22. Reusable OSM road-network preparation

Drivable network for the future Crew Dispatch and Routing component: pending in this build. Every public Overpass server was overloaded or down at packaging time (8 of 18 sub-queries cached). The download resumes with python osm_data_prep/download_osm.py --only roads. External Factors does not depend on it (see OSM_DATA_README.md). Coverage area: borough union + 1000 m. Simplified topology; largest weakly connected component retained; directionality (oneway, reversed), edge geometry and length preserved. Files: roads/nyc_drive.graphml (load with osmnx.load_graphml) and roads/nyc_drive.gpkg (layers nodes, edges). No routing, speeds or travel times are computed here.

Sparse attributes (for example maxspeed, lanes) are documented for later enrichment, such as osmnx.routing.add_edge_speeds with agreed defaults.

23. Academic decision register

Each decision lists the alternatives, evidence, rationale, limitations and **course

alignment** (DA = decision automation through business rules / knowledge-based reasoning;

KDDM = knowledge discovery and data mining; BRO = business-resource optimisation, which belongs

to Crew Dispatch and is deliberately not used here). All figures come from executed runs

(outputs/tables/, outputs/benchmarks/). No figure is invented.

D1. Scope: critical-facility proximity only (weather removed)

  • Alternatives: keep the weather sub-factor described in the 28 September shared reference; combine proximity with urgency.
  • Evidence: the task prompt sets the current scope (weather removed). The shared reference lists the External Factors output as "to be named by Mohammad".
  • Rationale: one well-defined geographic question gives a factor that is testable and easy to explain. The wx_* columns in the historical data are ignored (see data_validation_summary.json).
  • Limitations: the shared reference PDF still mentions weather and needs a group update.
  • Course: DA (a clean rule boundary).

D2. Data source: OpenStreetMap

  • Alternatives: NYC Open Data facility layers (DOE school points, DOHMH facilities, FDNY firehouses); commercial POI data.
  • Evidence: OSM gave all required categories in one schema and one acquisition: 4,445 de-duplicated facilities, 4,580 features in total (data/osm/manifest.json). OSM keeps polygon footprints for 1,998 of 4,580 features (44%), which the official point layers usually lack. The road network for Crew Dispatch comes from the same source.
  • Rationale: one open, versionable source (ODbL) with stable identifiers (way/123). Tag conventions were checked against the OSM wiki.
  • Limitations: volunteer data is incomplete and uneven. For example, only 97 hospitals are tagged, and some may be specialised (psychiatric) facilities. No official completeness audit was done. Facility recall is unknown.
  • Course: KDDM (data acquisition and quality assessment).

D3. All five boroughs plus a 2 km buffer

  • Alternatives: only the boroughs of interest; limit searches to the request's own borough.
  • Evidence: validate_osm.py confirms all five OSM borough relations are present and that every core category exists in every borough. 404 de-duplicated facilities (359 in core categories) lie outside NYC inside the buffer. Test 10 (facility across a borough line) and test 11 (facility outside NYC) pass. On the real cache, a Staten Island example found its nearest facility in Carteret, NJ.
  • Rationale: proximity is physical. Borough lines (and the state line) do not block an ambulance route or a school crossing. The buffer (2,000 m) is more than the ruleset needs (threshold 100 + maximum evaluable uncertainty 250 + coverage tolerance 100 = 450 m). The evaluator checks this when it loads.
  • Limitations: OSM borough relations include water, so "inside NYC" is administrative rather than land-only. Marble Hill is labelled BRONX in the 311 data but lies in Manhattan's OSM boundary (53 of the 58 borough mismatches).
  • Course: KDDM (coverage validation).

D4. Distances in metres in a projected CRS (EPSG:32118)

  • Alternatives: raw degree differences; haversine on a sphere; geodesic distance for every pair; UTM 18N.
  • Evidence: across 3,000 request-facility pairs, the maximum difference from WGS84 geodesic distance was 0.099 m (0.0012%), and at most 0.002 m within 250 m (benchmark_results.json). Naive degree subtraction overstates a 0.01° longitude step at 40.75°N by 31.8%.
  • Rationale: EPSG:32118 (NAD83 / New York Long Island) is the metric State Plane zone built for NYC. Planar distances are exact enough and enable vectorised GEOS queries.
  • Limitations: the CRS is NYC-specific. Reuse elsewhere needs a different metric CRS (configurable through metric_crs).
  • Course: knowledge representation (correct spatial semantics).

D5. Straight-line, not network, distance

  • Alternatives: walking or driving network distance; travel time.
  • Rationale: the question is whether a request is geographically adjacent to a facility, not how long a crew takes to get there. Network travel time belongs to Crew Dispatch and Routing (BRO: A*, Dijkstra), which reuses the prepared road graph.
  • Limitations: a facility across a river or a highway can be close in straight-line terms but socially or physically separated.
  • Course: a clear separation between DA (here) and BRO (dispatch).

D6. Polygon geometry preserved; distance to the geometry, not the centroid

  • Alternatives: convert everything to centroids; use points only.
  • Evidence: 1,998 of 4,580 features are polygons or multipolygons. Test 05 shows a request 100 m from a polygon edge but 150 m from its centroid, which only the boundary distance flags correctly. Test 04 gives 0 m for a request inside a hospital footprint. The real Mount Sinai example is inside the footprint (0 m).
  • Rationale: centroids misstate adjacency for large campuses (hospitals, school grounds). GEOS distance to a (Multi)Polygon is 0 inside, otherwise to the nearest boundary.
  • Duplicates: OSM often maps a facility twice (POI node plus building). The rules D1 (point within 15 m of a same-category polygon, compatible name), D2 (polygon ≥95% inside a same-category polygon) and D3 (same-name points within 15 m) flagged 135 duplicates. They are kept for audit (is_duplicate, duplicate_of) but excluded from evaluation. Duplicates never reduce the nearest distance, so the binary flag does not change. Only counts and evidence lists do.
  • Limitations: point-only facilities (for example, 171 of 351 fire-station features) are measured to the node, which typically sits at the building centre. This overstates the distance by roughly half the building depth.
  • Course: knowledge representation.

D7. Spatial indexing (STRtree per category)

  • Alternatives: brute-force distance to all facilities; a single index for all categories.
  • Evidence: 27x faster than brute force with identical results (max difference 0 m). On average 0.36 candidates per request survive the 100 m search, compared with 3,803 facilities checked by brute force. Single-request latency p50 is 0.144 ms; batch throughput is about 20.6k requests/s on the development machine.
  • Rationale: per-category trees support category-specific thresholds and "nearest per category" evidence.
  • Course: efficient knowledge-base querying.

D8. Explainable rules rather than a learned model

  • Alternatives: an ML classifier for "relevant proximity"; a weighted proximity score.
  • Evidence: there is no independent ground-truth label of "facility-relevant hazard", and outcome fields (outcome_class, etc.) are after-the-fact and do not measure proximity relevance.
  • Rationale: a declarative ruleset (config/proximity_rules.yaml) with rule identifiers, a structured evidence record and natural-language explanations gives a traceable binary decision. All 49,558 historical evaluations have a non-empty explanation and rule list, and every positive carries facility evidence (holdout_summary.json).
  • Course: DA (business rules / knowledge-based reasoning).

D9. Pure geographic design (Design A) selected; context-aware gating kept as opt-in

  • Alternatives: Design B, context-aware: (B1) category-specific radii, (B2) add transit stations, (B3) zero the factor for building-interior request types.
  • Evidence (validation, configuration_comparison_val.csv): A flags 26.2%. B1 (emergency sites at 150 m) adds 197 requests (agrees with A 97.3%). B2 (transit) adds 233 (96.8%). B3 removes 306 positives (95.8%): 16% of A's positives are interior housing or elevator requests.
  • Rationale: A is the simplest, fully request-type-independent and easy to interpret. B3 is spatially plausible (interior conditions are not in the public right of way), but it uses request type, which already drives Urgency. Adopting it unilaterally risks double counting. It is implemented (decision_mode: CONTEXT_AWARE) and tested, ready if the Urgency owner agrees. B1 has no outcome evidence that emergency sites need a wider radius. B2 behaves as a density proxy, because subway stations are so dense.
  • Limitations: A flags facilities that may be irrelevant to some complaints (for example, an apartment heat complaint next to a school).
  • Course: DA, with explicit interface design.

D10. How double counting with Urgency is prevented

  • In PURE_GEOGRAPHIC mode the request type never enters the computation (test: RT005 and RT080 at the same point give identical evidence and factor).
  • The output contains no urgency level, weight, score, rank or dispatch field. A recursive key scan in the tests enforces this.
  • Both critical_facility_nearby (pure geographic evidence) and external_factor (agreed final factor) are returned, so Urgency decides how proximity interacts with request type.
  • Rule identifiers name the facility category that triggered (for example, CRITICAL_PROXIMITY_SCHOOL), never a severity.

D11. Candidate thresholds and how they were evaluated

  • Candidates: 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 400, 500, 750, 1000 m. These are experimental values from immediate surroundings to a broad neighbourhood, not NYC policy.
  • Train exploration: the median nearest-core distance is 155 m. Trigger rate rises from 12.3% (50 m) to 28.8% (100 m), 48.4% (150 m), 73.8% (250 m) and 95.0% (500 m). Elasticity exceeds 1 up to 150 m. Schools are the sole trigger for about two thirds of flagged requests. A 15 m displacement flips 13% of positives at 100 m and 6% at 150 m.
  • Protocol: config/threshold_selection_protocol.yaml was fixed after train exploration and before any validation proximity result. It defines an admissible range (75–150 m) from the operational definition and from geocoding error, a knowledge-based prior (100 m), and criteria C1–C5 (decision agreement ≥95% and positive stability ≥85% under 15 m error, train-validation shift ≤5 pp, trigger rate ≤50%, borough max/min ratio ≤3).
  • Course: KDDM (sensitivity analysis, temporal validation).

D12. Final threshold: 100 m, universal across the six core categories

  • Evidence (validation): trigger rate 26.2% (train 28.8%, shift −2.6 pp), decision agreement 96.5%, positive stability 92.6%, borough ratio 2.95. All five criteria pass. 75 m fails C5 (ratio 3.30). 150 m fails C3 (shift −6.2 pp).
  • Hold-out (test, after freezing): 26.3% (shift +0.1 pp vs validation), agreement 96.2%, positive stability 92.3%, ratio 2.62. All within the pre-declared tolerances.
  • Operational meaning: "on the same block frontage, directly across the street, or at the adjacent intersection" (NYC short block ≈ 80 m, avenue right-of-way ≈ 30 m).
  • Status: a knowledge-based heuristic, empirically checked. It is not statistically optimal and not an official NYC threshold, because no outcome labels exist. The borough ratio (2.95) sits close to its 3.0 bound.
  • Course: DA + KDDM.

D13. Incomplete evaluations are null, never silently 0

  • Alternatives: default to 0; default to 1 ("safe" under shared rule 6).
  • Evidence: 2.5% of historical requests are incomplete: 1,157 with missing coordinates and 75 where the location uncertainty spans the threshold.
  • Rationale: a 0 claims "no facility nearby", which is false when the location is unknown. external_factor = null with incomplete_reason and needs_review = true keeps this honest. Shared rule 6 ("a failing component falls back to a safe default that does not lower anyone's score") is respected, because null contributes nothing. If Urgency needs an integer, to_integer_factor(result, null_policy) requires an explicit, agreed policy (ZERO_FLAGGED or ONE_FLAGGED) and flags every imputed value.
  • Location uncertainty: an interval rule is used. With uncertainty u ≤ 30 m the supplied point decides (POINT_ESTIMATE). With 30 < u ≤ 250 m the factor is set only when the whole uncertainty disc lies inside (margin ≥ u) or outside (margin < −u) the threshold. Otherwise it is null. With u > 250 m, or postal-code/borough precision, the result is INCOMPLETE. Default uncertainties per precision class are heuristic. Under a 120 m displacement, 24% of decisions flip at 100 m, which is why coarse locations cannot use the point estimate.
  • Course: knowledge-based reasoning under uncertainty.

D14. Road network prepared for future reuse (no routing here)

  • Rationale: Crew Dispatch and Routing needs a drivable graph. Downloading it once, with the same boundaries, CRS conventions and manifest, avoids duplicate acquisition and keeps the components consistent. No routing, A*, Dijkstra or travel-time logic is implemented here. Missing attributes (for example, sparse maxspeed) are documented in OSM_DATA_README.md for later enrichment.
  • Status: the road download was still incomplete at packaging time (8/18 sub-queries; every public Overpass server was overloaded or down). It is resumable with one command and shipped as a separate bundle. External Factors does not depend on it.
  • Course: a shared data layer for BRO (the separate component).

D15. Static visualisation separated from business logic

  • Rationale: maps and charts (visualization/, research/) only read cached data and the evaluator's outputs. The runtime package has no plotting, OSMnx or network dependency (test 29b checks that importing the evaluator loads neither osmnx nor requests). Static PNGs are reproducible and embeddable in the report. No live dashboard is built.

D16. Temporal split and leakage discipline

  • Evidence: the splits are chronological and do not overlap (train 2025-09-24 to 2026-05-20, val to 2026-07-17, test to 2026-09-16). closed_date, status, resolution_*, outcome_class, verified_outcome and resolution_hours are dropped as soon as the data load. Live inputs carrying them are ignored with a warning (tested).
  • Rationale: train for exploration, validation for selection, test touched once after freezing. No supervised training occurs, and no outcome is used to manufacture proximity labels.
  • Limitation: the sample is borough-stratified (about 10k per borough), so citywide rates are not volume-weighted to real 311 traffic.

24. Limitations

  • No ground truth. No label says whether a facility actually affected a request, so accuracy, precision, recall and F1 are not reported, and the trigger rate is not prediction quality. The threshold is defensible, not validated against outcomes.
  • OSM completeness is unknown. Facility recall and tagging quality vary (for example, 97 hospitals; some fire stations are mapped as nodes only). No comparison with official NYC registers was authorised.
  • Straight-line adjacency ignores barriers (rivers, highways, rail cuts) and building entrances.
  • Heuristic uncertainty defaults. The per-precision uncertainties are assumptions, not measured geocoder error. The historical precision proxy (address_type) is not the future Geolocation Resolution output.
  • Sample design. The historical sample is borough-stratified. Citywide rates are not volume-weighted. Repeated coordinates (repeat addresses) are frequent.
  • Borough equity margin. The selected threshold's borough ratio (2.95) is close to its 3.0 bound. The difference mostly reflects real facility density, not a defect.
  • Interface still open. Field names for External Factors are "to be named by Mohammad" in the shared reference. The null policy and any request-type gating need agreement with Urgency. The shared reference PDF still mentions weather.

25. Conclusions

The component gives a trustworthy, explainable geographic factor. It is a binary statement that a qualifying critical facility's geometry is within 100 m of a reliably located request, returned with the evidence behind it, and it explicitly abstains when the location does not support a decision. It is a legitimate knowledge-based reasoning component: domain knowledge (facility relevance, street geometry, measurement error) is encoded as transparent, versioned rules, and uncertainty is handled by explicit interval reasoning. It is a knowledge-discovery exercise as well: the rules were explored, stress-tested and selected on real data under a pre-declared, leakage-free temporal protocol, and confirmed on a hold-out split. The historical data support that the rule is stable over time, robust to typical geocoding error, informative (about a quarter of requests flagged) and evenly behaved across boroughs within the stated bound. They do not establish that proximity causes harm or that 100 m is optimal for any outcome. That would need labelled outcomes, which do not exist yet.

Map and facility data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0. Historical requests: supplied NYC311 project sample. Generated by reports/build_report.py from executed outputs.
